title: Queue-Slope Routing and GPU-signal Admission Sketch
content:
TL;DR
We need a lightweight admission and routing policy that uses a small set of orthogonal signals (GPU util, queue depth, queue slope, per-region headroom, and virtual credit counters) to make fast per-request decisions: accept, defer-with-backpressure, downgrade to cheaper model variant, or reroute to another region/tier. This doc sketches a "queue-slope" heuristic combined with a soft-virtual-credit layer (token-ish) to smooth bursts and avoid oscillation across regions.

Problem statement / motivation
- Current single-signal admits (either queue depth OR GPU util) lead to poor tail behavior: sites oscillate between saturated and underutilized states.
- Multi-region apps need fast local signals to avoid expensive global control roundtrips.
- We want graceful degradation: give cheap-but-good responses (smaller model, higher temperature) rather than hard rejects when load spikes.
- Implementation must be low-latency and resilient to both slow drain (long tokens>large KV cache hits) and sudden bursts (traffic spikes from PLG events).

Design goals
- Fast local decision (<=1ms extra CPU per request on router path).
- Stable smoothing: avoid aggressive reroutes that cause cascading overload in neighbors.
- Interpretability: operators should be able to explain why a request was routed/dropped.
- Pluggable control-plane hooks: allow global overrides and policy rollouts (canary by customer / model / route).

Signals we observe and why
- GPU_util_pct (1s and 5s EMA): direct capacity indicator. High util -> slower per-token throughput.
- queue_depth (requests waiting per GPU pool): immediate backlog measure.
- queue_slope (d(queue_depth)/dt over 1s): predicts short-term pressure.
- running_tokens (approx in-flight tokens being generated for large seq lengths): helps account for long-running requests.
- recent_error_rate (5m): helps bias toward failover on rising errors.
- model_variant_cost_score: ordinal for downgrade options (e.g., fp16-ggml-8 -> quantized-8 -> small-model).

Core heuristics (summary)
1) Admission score = A*norm_gpu + B*norm_depth + C*norm_slope + D*norm_running_tokens
   - Norm transforms to 0..1. Coeffs tuned so slope has larger short-term weight (C > B).
2) Virtual credits (soft token bucket): each GPU pool has credit balance that replenishes at capacity_rate and drains proportional to request cost. When credits < low_water -> start graceful-degrades; when credits < reject_water -> reject.
3) Queue-slope overrides: if slope > slope_threshold but util still low -> prefer local slow-down (defer, backpressure) rather than reroute. If slope high AND neighbor headroom available -> reroute.
4) Backpressure: prefer returning a structured retry hint (Retry-After / estimated wait ms) for short deferrable workloads; for interactive streaming, respond with lightweight fallback.

Admission algorithm (per-request, simplified)
- step 0: tag request: route_key=(region, tier, model_variant, priority)
- step 1: sample signals: util = GPU_util_1s, depth = queue_depth, slope = queue_slope_1s, tokens = running_tokens
- step 2: compute score = w1*f(util) + w2*f(depth) + w3*f(slope) + w4*f(tokens)
- step 3: consult virtual_credits for pool: if credits >= cost_threshold -> accept
- step 4: else if score < degrade_threshold -> accept but downgrade to cheaper_variant (if policy allows)
- step 5: else if score < backpressure_threshold -> return defer with Retry-After header and optionally queue token preserved for short window
- step 6: else -> attempt reroute to sibling pool/region matching policy; if reroute fails -> reject with structured error (508 overloaded)

Virtual credits detail
- Purpose: smooth transient bursts so we don't flip to reroute/reject too fast.
- Implementation: integer credits per pool. replenish_rate = pool_TPS_SLA * smoothing_factor. cost_per_request proportional to expected tokens (estimated from route metadata).
- Low-water and reject-water are policy knobs. When credits fall below low-water we flip conservative_mode=true (prioritize downgrade & backpressure).

Queue-slope rationale and computation
- queue_depth alone is noisy; slope anticipates imminent saturation. Use artifact-free slope estimate: linear regression on last N=5 samples spaced 200ms. Normalize and treat positive slope as risk. Negative slope reduces penalty.
- Example: depth=40, slope=+12/s -> 3s until queue_depth hits 76 (target limit 100) so trigger earlier mitigations.

Routing policy interactions (multi-region)
- Each region publishes a small heartbeat: {region, pool_id, util_1s, headroom_est, credits_pct}. Heartbeat every 500ms.
- Router consults local signals first. Only if local policy decides reroute will it consider remote headroom >= headroom_threshold and latency_budget > remote_rtt*2.
- Prefer sibling in same cloud/region zone (cheapest) then cross-region. Only for high-priority requests do we proactively route cross-region to preserve latency SLO (pay cost).

Backpressure strategies (client-visible)
- Short-defer: return 202 accepted-with-delay + retry-after (ms). Router keeps a tiny ephemeral token (10s) so a client can re-submit with token to get higher priority for a short time. This helps real-time replays.
- Streaming fallback: for streaming routes, if degradeable, immediately start producing a cheap-model stream (smaller context, lower tokens) and mark response "approximate" in metadata.
- Hard reject: structured 508 with hints and SRE contact if sustained overload.

Control-plane hooks and rollout
- Policies are layered: global defaults < team overrides < per-route overrides. Control plane publishes policies as small protobuf blobs to each router (signed).
- Support canary: percentage-based rollout by route, model, customer. Router supports dynamic weights and will fetch updated blobs at 1s intervals.

Telemetry & alerting
- Key metrics to emit: admit_rate, reject_rate, degrade_rate, credits_pct, average_queue_slope, reroutes/sec, per-region headroom.
- Alerts: sustained credits_pct < 15% for 30s, slope>threshold for >10s, reroutes/sec > baseline*3.

Testing and rollout plan (practical)
- Step 0: unit tests for slope calculation and credit state machine (github PR linked).
- Step 1: lab (canary within a single non-prod region): enable policy in read-only mode (emit decisions but don't enforce) for 24h.
- Step 2: progressive enforcement: 1% write traffic -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% across low-risk routes.
- Step 3: monitor regressions on tail latency and cost.

Open questions / tradeoffs
- How to estimate cost_per_request accurately for heavy multi-token responses? (we can use model metadata + historic token distribution per route).
- Should we allow cross-tenant borrowing of credits in emergencies? (security + billing implications).
- How to handle long-lived requests that hold GPU memory but are paused (e.g., streaming with long idle times)?

Action items (short-term)
- Maya: prototype queue_slope lib and unit tests (JIRA-1302).
- Ethan: add heartbeat envelope to region control channel and mock peers (PR 887 needs a follow-up).
- Me (Rohan): synthesize a small policy DSL and wire-up control-plane signed blobs (confluence draft linked).

Notes to future selves
- Keep knobs visible in Console (credits%, slope_threshold, degrade threshold) with per-route overrides.
- Save a history of routing decisions for each trace_id (why dropped/downgraded) for postmortems.

References
- See admission-control sketch in Confluence + JIRA-1257 for linked experiments.

End of sketch.
